title: Vishvamitra, the seer who saw the Gayatri
word: the Gayatri and the peace chants
hook: a king becomes a sage among sages, and who the who is
carry: the rishis saw the verse; the god stirs minds
tomorrow: the verse has one word left, and it asks for something. what?

segments.voice: Yesterday, dhimahi: the Gayatri prays as we, even alone, and Satyakama was taken into the line. Today the week comes back around, with three small words.

Half the confusion in any group chat is pronouns. He said he'd bring it. Which he? The Gayatri has the same knot in its second line: dhiyo yo nah. Yo means who. So who is the who: the radiance, or the god? The answer is the god. And the man who first heard the verse never claimed to be it.
screen: `HE SAID HE'D BRING IT. WHICH HE?`

segments.voice: Here's how a reader knows. Yah, who, is masculine. The radiance is neuter. So who points to the god, Savitr. Dhiyo: thoughts, many of them. Nah: our. Who, our thoughts. Now finish the week's story. After he left his throne, Vishvamitra's austerities kept breaking. Once it was anger: in the Ramayana, he curses a nymph sent to distract him, feels his power drain away, and vows never to be angry again. Years later, at the end of a long fast, a stranger begs for his food, and he gives it all away without a word. Then the gods hail him as a brahmarshi, a sage among sages, and he asks for one more voice. Vasishtha, the sage whose staff had beaten him, says it too, and the old rivals become friends. Tradition remembers him as the seer of the Gayatri. Seer is the right word. Hindus call the Vedas shruti, what was heard: the rishis didn't invent the mantras, they saw them and heard them. So even the verse's own seer isn't its who. The who is the god, asked to stir our thoughts. The week, end to end: a king's lesson and two verbs. Tat, pointing to Brahman. Savitr's sun at sandhya. Varenyam, the good chosen. The radiance nobody owns. Dhimahi, always we. And who, our thoughts. One word is left.
screen: `YAH IS MASCULINE: IT MEANS THE GOD.` · `VISHVAMITRA GIVES UP ANGER.` · `VASISHTHA CALLS HIM BRAHMARSHI.` · `SHRUTI: WHAT WAS HEARD.` · then, large: `THE SEER SAW. THE GOD STIRS.`

segments.voice: Listen for one sound that keeps going on its own: a fan, traffic, a fridge, rain. Let it be the only thing you follow. When a thought pulls you off, notice it, one of the many, and come back to the sound.
The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece, lightly: dhiyo yo nah, who, our thoughts, and the who is the god, not the seer.

segments.voice: Hold onto this: the rishis saw the verse; the god stirs minds, ours included. A week, done.

howItsDone: In some families the Gayatri is given at the sacred-thread ceremony and said at home each day; others teach it openly to anyone. Its invocation names Vishvamitra as its rishi, the seer who saw it. Teachers who explain it word by word show that yah, who, points to Savitr.

chat.says: Dad says we keep the Gayatri for home, not stages. fine. but who's the 'who' in it?
options: the god: yo is masculine and the radiance is neuter. not even Vishvamitra, who saw it, is the who.
the light: yo points to the nearest noun, and bhargo is right there.
the people praying: yo means you, the one saying it.
chat.meaning: Yah, who, is masculine; the radiance is neuter. So the who is the god Savitr, asked to stir our thoughts. Vishvamitra is its seer, not its who: Hindus hold the rishis saw the Vedas.

Grammar stated: dhiyaḥ accusative plural of dhī; yaḥ masculine relative referring to Savitr (not to neuter bhargas); naḥ enclitic 'our/us'; -aḥ becoming o before voiced y and n. Confirm wording for learners.
